title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (Literature Review) and Ch. 3 (System Design): the original definition of RAG, a parametric generator paired with a non-parametric retrieved memory. This is the baseline pattern MedBridge builds on before it adds the Context and Evidence gates.
summary: The paper pairs a pretrained seq2seq generator with a dense retriever over Wikipedia. Retrieved passages are treated as a latent variable, and both parts are fine-tuned end to end. It reports better open-domain QA results and more factual generation than parametric-only models. Its retrieval is always on and it has no way to abstain, so it cannot refuse when the evidence is weak. MedBridge's gates are built to fill that gap.

title: Survey of Hallucination in Natural Language Generation
use_in_report: Ch. 1 (Problem Statement) and Ch. 2: defines intrinsic vs extrinsic hallucination and motivates why an unguarded generator is unsafe for cardiology answers. Also supports the hallucination taxonomy used in the evaluation chapter.
summary: A broad survey of hallucination across NLG tasks such as summarisation, dialogue, QA and data-to-text. It separates intrinsic hallucination (contradicting the source) from extrinsic hallucination (content the source cannot verify), and reviews metrics and mitigation methods. Most of its coverage predates instruction-tuned LLMs, so it says little about them or about clinical RAG settings.

title: A Survey on Hallucination in Large Language Models: Principles, Taxonomy, Challenges, and Open Questions
use_in_report: Ch. 2: an up-to-date LLM-specific hallucination taxonomy (factuality vs faithfulness), including hallucinations that arise inside RAG pipelines. Justifies treating retrieval failure and generation unfaithfulness as separate risks, which MedBridge handles at the pre- and post-retrieval gates.
summary: Surveys hallucination in LLMs specifically. It splits errors into factuality and faithfulness types, traces their causes to data, training and inference, and reviews detection benchmarks and mitigation methods. It has a dedicated discussion of retrieval-augmented systems and their remaining failure modes. As a survey it does not evaluate anything in a medical domain or on locally hosted models.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (Related Work, adaptive RAG) and the design-justification section: the closest prior work to MedBridge's gates, since it decides when to retrieve and critiques relevance and support. Used to contrast learned reflection tokens with MedBridge's explicit, auditable gates that need no fine-tuning.
summary: Self-RAG fine-tunes a single LM to emit special reflection tokens. These tokens decide whether to retrieve, judge whether passages are relevant, and judge whether each output segment is supported. At inference the tokens steer retrieval and segment selection, which improves factuality and citation accuracy. The method needs a custom-trained generator and has no explicit abstain or escalate action, which limits it in a safety-critical clinical tool built on off-the-shelf local models.

title: Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and Ch. 3 (Evidence Gate design): prior work on scoring retrieved documents after retrieval and acting on that score (correct / incorrect / ambiguous). This is directly analogous to MedBridge's ANSWER/GENERALIZE/ABSTAIN/ESCALATE decision.
summary: CRAG adds a lightweight retrieval evaluator that scores how good the retrieved documents are. A confidence band triggers one of three actions: refine the documents, discard them and fall back to web search, or combine both. It also filters documents with a decompose-then-recompose step. The paper is plug-and-play but still always produces an answer and relies on open web search, so it is not suitable for an offline clinical assistant that must be able to abstain or escalate.

title: Chain-of-Verification Reduces Hallucination in Large Language Models
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (post-hoc verification approaches): an example of prompting-only self-verification. Contrasted with MedBridge's evidence-grounded gate, which checks against retrieved guideline text rather than the model's own knowledge.
summary: CoVe has the model draft an answer, plan verification questions, answer them independently so they are not biased by the draft, and then write a revised answer. This reduces hallucinated facts in list QA, closed-book QA and long-form biographies. Verification uses only the model's own parametric knowledge, so shared misconceptions survive it, and the extra calls add latency on small local models.

title: RARR: Researching and Revising What Language Models Say, Using Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (attribution and post-hoc editing): supports the argument that outputs should be attributable to evidence. Contrasted with MedBridge's choice to gate before generation instead of repairing afterwards.
summary: RARR takes any LM's output, generates search queries about its claims, retrieves evidence, and edits unsupported content. It then attaches an attribution report while trying to keep the original text intact. It improves attribution with little loss of fluency. Because it repairs text after the fact using web search, it cannot stop an unsafe answer from being produced, which matters in a clinical setting.

title: SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and Ch. 6 (Evaluation): a reference-free hallucination detector based on sampling consistency, discussed as an alternative or complementary signal to MedBridge's NLI- and judge-based evaluation.
summary: SelfCheckGPT samples several responses from a black-box LLM and checks whether each sentence of the main answer is consistent with the samples. It uses BERTScore, QA, n-gram, NLI and prompting variants, on the idea that hallucinated facts vary across samples. It needs no external knowledge base. It costs many generations per query, and it cannot catch confident errors that the model repeats consistently, which retrieval grounding can catch.

title: FActScore: Fine-grained Atomic Evaluation of Factual Precision in Long Form Text Generation
venue: Proceedings of the 2023 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing
use_in_report: Ch. 6 (Evaluation methodology): justifies breaking answers into atomic claims and checking each against a knowledge source. This underpins MedBridge's claim-level NLI support scoring against retrieved guideline passages.
summary: FActScore splits a long-form generation into atomic facts and reports the fraction supported by a trusted source (Wikipedia in the paper). It also offers an automated estimator that tracks human judgements closely. Biographies show that even strong commercial LLMs make many unsupported claims. The metric measures precision only, not completeness, and its quality depends on the coverage of the reference corpus, here a curated cardiology guideline set.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Large Language Models: A Survey
use_in_report: Ch. 2: organises the field into naive, advanced and modular RAG and covers retrieval, augmentation and evaluation components. Used to place MedBridge's hybrid retrieval, reranking and gating within modular RAG.
summary: A wide survey that traces RAG from naive retrieve-then-read pipelines to advanced methods (query rewriting, reranking) and modular designs. It reviews retrieval sources, granularity, augmentation stages, and evaluation benchmarks and metrics. It is a general-domain overview without empirical comparison, and it remains an unrefereed preprint that its authors label ongoing work.

title: Know Your Limits: A Survey of Abstention in Large Language Models
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and Ch. 3 (Dual Answerability Gate rationale): the main reference for treating abstention as a first-class output. Supports MedBridge's ABSTAIN/ESCALATE outcomes and its evaluation of over- and under-abstention.
summary: Frames LLM abstention from three angles: the query (is it answerable or safe), the model (is it confident), and human values (should it answer). It catalogues abstention methods across pretraining, alignment and inference, along with the related benchmarks and metrics, and points to open gaps in how abstention is evaluated. Being a survey, it gives no domain-specific thresholds; MedBridge must calibrate those itself for cardiology.

title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 30 (NIPS 2017)
use_in_report: Ch. 3 (theoretical basis of the Evidence Gate) and Ch. 6 (risk-coverage analysis): formal grounding for trading coverage against risk by rejecting low-confidence inputs. This is the principle behind MedBridge's abstain thresholds and its risk-coverage curves.
summary: The paper builds a selective classifier from a trained network plus a confidence threshold. The threshold is calibrated so that, with high probability, the error rate on accepted inputs stays below a target risk. It demonstrates the guarantees on image classification (CIFAR and ImageNet). The work concerns classification with softmax or MC-dropout confidence, not free-text generation, so MedBridge adapts the idea to retrieval-evidence scores.

title: Conformal Prediction: A Gentle Introduction
venue: Foundations and Trends in Machine Learning
identifier: arXiv:2107.07511 (arXiv title: A Gentle Introduction to Conformal Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification)
use_in_report: Ch. 3 / Future Work: background on distribution-free calibration of decision thresholds. Supports the claim that gate thresholds can be calibrated on held-out data to bound error rates.
summary: A tutorial introduction to conformal prediction. It shows how to wrap any pretrained model so that its prediction sets have guaranteed finite-sample coverage under exchangeability, and covers conformal risk control and handling distribution shift. The guarantees are marginal rather than per-query and assume calibration data similar to deployment, which a small clinical test set may not satisfy.

title: Conformal Language Modeling
use_in_report: Ch. 2 / Future Work: shows conformal guarantees can be carried over to generative LMs, including flagging individually reliable sub-claims (e.g., radiology reports). Supports proposing statistically calibrated thresholds for MedBridge's gates.
summary: Extends conformal prediction to LM generation. The method calibrates a sampling stopping rule and a rejection rule, so that the returned set of candidate responses contains an acceptable one with a user-chosen probability. It can also mark individual phrases as reliable with guarantees. It needs repeated sampling and an admission function for what counts as acceptable, which is costly on local hardware and needs labelled clinical calibration data.

title: Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and Ch. 3: evidence that LLM self-assessed confidence (P(True), P(IK)) is partly informative but imperfect. Justifies MedBridge basing answerability on external retrieval evidence rather than on the model's own confidence alone.
summary: Shows that large LMs are fairly well calibrated on multiple-choice questions when the format is right. Models can be trained to predict whether they know an answer (P(IK)) and to score their own proposed answers (P(True)). Calibration weakens out of distribution and for smaller models. The experiments use large proprietary models, so the findings may not hold for the small local models MedBridge runs.

title: Judging LLM-as-a-Judge with MT-Bench and Chatbot Arena
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 36 (NeurIPS 2023), Datasets and Benchmarks Track
use_in_report: Ch. 6 (Evaluation methodology): justifies using an LLM judge for hallucination grading. It also documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases, which motivates pairing the judge with an independent NLI judge and human spot checks.
summary: Introduces MT-Bench and the crowdsourced Chatbot Arena, and studies strong LLMs such as GPT-4 as automatic judges of chat answers. GPT-4 agrees with human preferences at roughly the level humans agree with each other. The paper also documents position, verbosity and self-enhancement biases and limited judge reasoning on maths. The study covers general chat quality rather than clinical factual correctness.

title: LLM Evaluators Recognize and Favor Their Own Generations
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 37 (NeurIPS 2024)
use_in_report: Ch. 6 (threats to validity): justifies using a judge model from a different family than the generator, plus a non-LLM NLI judge, to reduce self-preference bias in hallucination scoring.
summary: Shows that LLMs such as GPT-4 and Llama 2 can tell their own outputs apart from other models' and from humans' outputs at better-than-chance rates. They also rate their own outputs higher than humans would. Fine-tuning experiments find that stronger self-recognition goes with stronger self-preference, consistent with a causal link. Experiments use summarisation tasks, so the size of the bias on medical QA judging is not established.

title: Large language models encode clinical knowledge
use_in_report: Ch.2 Literature Review (medical LLMs): shows that general LLMs can store medical knowledge but still fall short on harm, bias and factuality in human evaluation. This motivates MedBridge's safety-first design and its evaluation along several axes.
summary: Introduces the MultiMedQA benchmark (six existing QA sets plus HealthSearchQA) and a clinician rating framework covering factuality, reasoning, possible harm and bias. Uses it to evaluate Flan-PaLM and the instruction-prompt-tuned Med-PaLM. Med-PaLM reached state-of-the-art multiple-choice accuracy, yet human review still found gaps against clinicians. The models are large, closed and non-retrieval, so the paper does not cover the local RAG or abstention setting that MedBridge targets.

title: Toward expert-level medical question answering with large language models
use_in_report: Ch.2 Literature Review: state of the art in medical QA (Med-PaLM 2, about 86.5% on MedQA). Also supports the claim that even high-scoring models need adversarial safety testing, which motivates MedBridge's evidence gate and ESCALATE path.
summary: Med-PaLM 2 combines a stronger base model, medical fine-tuning, ensemble refinement and chain-of-retrieval, reaching up to 86.5% on MedQA. In pairwise ratings, physicians preferred it to physician answers on eight of nine axes, and it was tested on new adversarial question sets. It is a proprietary cloud model whose benchmarks are mostly exam-style, so it does not show how a small local model behaves with deterministic triage and abstention.

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2024
use_in_report: Ch.2 (medical RAG) and Ch.3 Methodology: closest prior benchmark for medical RAG. Supports choosing hybrid lexical+dense retrieval with fusion, and grounds the discussion of lost-in-the-middle effects and how many snippets to pass to the generator.
summary: Introduces MIRAGE, a benchmark of 7,663 medical questions, and MedRAG, a toolkit for comparing combinations of corpora, retrievers and LLMs (41 configurations). MedRAG improved six LLMs by up to 18% over chain-of-thought prompting. The authors also report log-linear scaling with the number of snippets and a lost-in-the-middle effect. All evaluation uses multiple-choice questions that must be answered, so answerability gating, abstention and conversational context are not covered, which are MedBridge's focus.

title: Med-HALT: Medical Domain Hallucination Test for Large Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 27th Conference on Computational Natural Language Learning (CoNLL)
use_in_report: Ch.2 (hallucination in medical LLMs) and Ch.5 Evaluation: prior hallucination benchmark. Its false-confidence and 'none of the above' tests relate to MedBridge's ABSTAIN behaviour and its hallucination-rate metric.
summary: Med-HALT is a multinational benchmark built from medical exam questions. It has reasoning hallucination tests (false confidence, none-of-the-above, fake questions) and memory tests (for example, recovering PubMed links and titles). The authors evaluated models including text-davinci, GPT-3.5, LLaMA-2, MPT and Falcon. The tests are mostly closed-book and exam-style, so they do not measure grounding against retrieved evidence or refusal in open patient dialogue.

title: Language Models are Surprisingly Fragile to Drug Names in Biomedical Benchmarks
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
use_in_report: Ch.2 and Ch.3: shows that LLMs are brittle to brand vs generic drug names, which matter in antihypertensive medication questions. This justifies BM25 (lexical) retrieval and synonym/alias handling alongside dense retrieval, and robustness checks in the evaluation.
summary: Builds RABBITS, a physician-annotated set of brand-to-generic drug-name swaps applied to MedQA and MedMCQA. Both open and API LLMs lost about 1-10% accuracy after the swap, and the authors trace part of this to benchmark contamination in pre-training corpora. The study covers only multiple-choice accuracy, so it does not show how name fragility affects retrieval-grounded answers.

title: Large language models in medicine
use_in_report: Ch.1 Introduction and Ch.2: general background on how LLMs/chatbots are built and their clinical strengths and limitations (hallucination, accountability). Frames the problem MedBridge addresses.
summary: A primer for clinicians that explains how LLM chatbots such as ChatGPT are developed and fine-tuned. It surveys clinical, educational and research uses and weighs efficiency gains against risks such as inaccuracy and misuse. As a narrative review it offers no experimental evidence on specific safety mechanisms such as retrieval gating or abstention.

title: Large language models propagate race-based medicine
use_in_report: Ch.2 (safety/bias risks) and Ch.6 Limitations/Ethics: evidence that commercial LLMs reproduce debunked race-based clinical claims, for example in eGFR and other calculations. Supports grounding answers in curated guideline evidence and discussing bias as a residual risk.
summary: The authors put nine questions to four commercial LLMs, five times each. The questions came from discussion among four physicians and from earlier work on race-based misconceptions held by medical trainees. Every model produced some race-based, inaccurate content, and its answers changed across repeated runs. The study is small and qualitative, and it tests ungrounded chat models rather than retrieval-constrained systems.

title: Almanac — Retrieval-Augmented Language Models for Clinical Medicine
use_in_report: Ch.2 (retrieval-augmented clinical LLMs): closest clinical RAG system with clinician evaluation of factuality, completeness and adversarial safety. Serves as the comparison point for MedBridge's grounded answering and safety evaluation.
summary: Almanac connects an LLM to curated medical resources so it can answer guideline and treatment questions. Eight board-certified clinicians and two other health care practitioners compared it with ChatGPT-4, Bing and Bard on 314 questions across nine specialties. Almanac scored better on factuality, completeness, user preference and adversarial safety. It depends on a cloud LLM and has no explicit pre-retrieval context check or calibrated abstain/escalate decision; MedBridge adds both.

title: A framework to assess clinical safety and hallucination rates of LLMs for medical text summarisation
use_in_report: Ch.5 Evaluation design: precedent for clinician-defined error taxonomies (hallucination vs omission, major vs minor), sentence-level annotation and clinical-harm grading. Informs MedBridge's hallucination labels and severity-weighted safety metrics.
summary: The paper proposes four parts: an error taxonomy, an iterative experiment structure, a clinical-safety harm assessment, and a review interface called CREOLA, all for LLM-generated clinical notes. Across 18 configurations and 12,999 clinician-annotated sentences, it measured a 1.47% hallucination rate and a 3.45% omission rate. Changes to prompts and workflows brought major errors down. The work covers summarising consultation transcripts, not open-ended patient QA with retrieval and abstention.

title: Medical Hallucinations in Foundation Models and Their Impact on Healthcare
identifier: arXiv:2503.05777 (v1 26 Feb 2025; v2 2 Nov 2025); medRxiv 10.1101/2025.02.28.25323115 (medRxiv title uses the singular 'Medical Hallucination')
use_in_report: Ch.2 (hallucination taxonomy) and Ch.1 problem statement: definition of medical hallucination as output that is unsupported or wrong in a way that could change clinical decisions. Also its finding that general models out-performed medical-specialised ones, relevant to MedBridge's choice of a general local LLM plus grounding.
summary: The paper defines and categorises medical hallucinations and reviews detection and mitigation methods, including retrieval-augmented generation and uncertainty quantification. It benchmarks 11 foundation models on seven hallucination tasks. General-purpose models gave more hallucination-free answers than medical-specialised ones (median 76.6% vs 51.3%). It also reports a global survey of 70 clinicians. It has not been peer reviewed, and its benchmarks are not specific to cardiology or to local models.

title: Comparing Physician and Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses to Patient Questions Posted to a Public Social Media Forum
use_in_report: Ch.1 Motivation: patient demand for and perceived quality of chatbot answers to health questions. Ch.6 Discussion: rated quality and empathy are not the same as verified correctness or safety, which motivates MedBridge's gates.
summary: This cross-sectional study took 195 patient questions from Reddit's r/AskDocs that a verified physician had answered. Licensed health care professionals compared ChatGPT's answers with the physicians' answers and preferred the chatbot in 78.6% of 585 evaluations, rating it higher on quality and empathy. Chatbot answers were about four times longer (211 vs 52 words), which may have revealed or swayed the raters. Accuracy was rated subjectively rather than checked against evidence sources, so the study says little about hallucination risk.

title: An automated framework for assessing how well LLMs cite relevant medical references
identifier: arXiv:2402.02008 (earlier preprint titled 'How well do LLMs cite relevant medical references? An evaluation framework and analyses'); PMID:40240349; PMCID:PMC12003634
use_in_report: Ch.5 Evaluation: precedent for automated, LLM-based checking that each cited source supports each statement, validated by doctors. Supports MedBridge's citation-faithfulness checks and LLM-as-judge plus NLI judge design.
summary: SourceCheckup is an agent-based pipeline that breaks LLM answers into statements and checks whether each cited source is relevant and supports them. Across seven LLMs, 800 questions and about 58,000 statement-source pairs, 50-90% of responses were not fully supported by the sources they cited. Even GPT-4o with web search left about 30% of statements unsupported. The judge is itself an LLM, and the study audits citations rather than proposing a gating mechanism.

title: Opportunities and challenges for ChatGPT and large language models in biomedicine and health
use_in_report: Ch.2 Literature Review: survey of how LLMs are used for biomedical information retrieval, QA and summarisation. Its discussion of made-up content and patient-data privacy supports MedBridge's choices of grounding, local deployment and PII redaction.
summary: This survey reviews LLM use in five biomedical areas: information retrieval, question answering, text summarisation, information extraction and medical education. It finds that LLMs beat earlier methods on text-generation tasks but gave only modest gains elsewhere. It names fabricated output and legal and privacy risks around patient data as the main concerns. It runs no new experiments and was written before most work on medical RAG and abstention, so it does not cover answerability gating.

title: Evaluating Retrieval-Augmented Generation Variants for Clinical Decision Support: Hallucination Mitigation and Secure On-Premises Deployment
use_in_report: Review-1 row (1) 'Electronics/MDPI 2025: retrieval grounding cuts hallucination, not sufficient alone'. Match confidence MEDIUM-HIGH. Cite in Ch.2 Literature Review (RAG safety) for the claim that grounding lowers hallucination but leaves a residual rate (best variant still 5.8%), so extra verification layers are needed. Also cite in the design-justification chapter: its best retrieval came from a Haystack pipeline (dense DPR + BM25 + cross-encoder reranking) and from hybrid Reciprocal Rank Fusion, and it recommends on-premises deployment with encryption, provenance tagging and audit trails. This is close to MedBridge's retrieval stack and privacy design.
summary: The paper compares twelve kinds of RAG pipeline (dense, sparse, hybrid, graph-based, multimodal, self-reflective, adaptive and security-focused, among others) on 250 de-identified patient cases, measuring retrieval quality (P@5, MRR, nDCG@10), hallucination rate and latency. A dense+BM25+cross-encoder pipeline and RRF hybrid fusion retrieved best. Self-reflective RAG had the lowest hallucination rate, 5.8%, which is still above zero, so the author proposes retrieval-confidence thresholds, chain-of-thought verification and external fact-checking. Limitation for MedBridge: it is a single-author study on case vignettes and has no formal rule for when to answer, abstain or escalate.
source_checked: https://api.crossref.org/works/10.3390/electronics14214227 (also https://api.openalex.org/works/doi:10.3390/electronics14214227; the MDPI page returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher)

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) vs. Fine-Tuning: A Systematic Review of Hallucination Mitigation in Medical LLMs
identifier: Authorea preprint v1 posted 2026-01-21 (Crossref posted-content, publisher Wiley)
use_in_report: Review-1 row (3) 'Authorea 2025: RAG alone doesn't guarantee safety without verification'. Match confidence LOW. The record exists, but it was posted 21 Jan 2026, not 2025. Its indexed abstract also calls RAG the better strategy for clinical safety and the factual guardrail for patient-facing use, which does not clearly support the row's claim that RAG alone is not enough. Use it only if the team confirms this is the paper they meant. Otherwise drop the row or support the claim with rows 1 and 2.
summary: This is a single-author systematic review, posted as a preprint, that compares RAG and fine-tuning for reducing hallucination in medical LLMs. According to the search-index abstract snippet, it draws on 50 peer-reviewed studies from 2023 to 2025. It finds that RAG lowers hallucination by using up-to-date knowledge without retraining, while fine-tuning adapts better to clinical style but is costly and risks catastrophic forgetting, and it recommends hybrid systems. Limitation: it is not peer reviewed, and the full text and abstract could not be opened (Authorea returned 403; Crossref and OpenAlex have no abstract), so this summary rests only on the indexed snippet.

title: Prompt Injection Attacks on Large Language Models: A Survey of Attack Methods, Root Causes, and Defense Strategies
use_in_report: Review-1 row (4) 'CMC 2025: structural input isolation defends against prompt injection'. Match confidence MEDIUM. The DOI contains 2025 and the paper was accepted in Nov 2025, which probably explains the '2025' label, but the issue is dated 2026. Its defense section covers separating instructions from data (StruQ, Spotlighting, SecAlign). Cite in Ch.2 and in the security design section to justify MedBridge keeping retrieved and user text apart from system instructions. Also cite it to note that prompt-engineering defenses come with no formal security guarantees.
summary: This systematic review of 128 peer-reviewed studies (2022–2025) covers prompt-injection attacks, their root causes and defenses. It traces the problem mainly to LLMs being unable to tell instructions from data. It reports that input preprocessing detects about 60–80% of attacks and that advanced architectural defenses block up to about 95% of known patterns. It also notes that filters can be evaded by obfuscation and that prompt-engineering defenses lack formal guarantees. Limitation: it is a survey with no new experiments, and it mentions medical settings only briefly, through one cited example of injection via medical images.

title: MedCite: Can Language Models Generate Verifiable Text for Medicine?
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2025
area: Citation verifiability in medical generation (Review-1 row 5)
use_in_report: Review-1 row (5) 'ACL Findings 2025: citation verifiability in medical generation'. Match confidence HIGH. Cite in Ch.2 for the claim that medical LLM answers need citations that can be checked, and in the Evidence Gate and citation design section as prior work on generating and evaluating citations in medical QA.
summary: MedCite is an end-to-end framework for designing and evaluating citation generation in medical LLM answers. It adds a multi-pass retrieval-and-citation method that beats strong baselines on citation precision and recall, and its automatic citation evaluation agrees well with expert annotations. Limitation for MedBridge: it checks whether citations support the text but does not decide whether the system should answer at all, so it has no abstain or escalate gate.

title: Controlling Risk of Retrieval-augmented Generation: A Counterfactual Prompting Framework
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: EMNLP 2024
use_in_report: Review-1 row (6) 'ACL/EMNLP Findings 2024: risk-controlled RAG generation framework'. Match confidence HIGH. Cite in Ch.2 and in the Evidence Gate design as the closest prior work on RAG systems that refuse low-confidence questions, which supports MedBridge's ABSTAIN outcome. Also cite it in the evaluation chapter as a precedent for its risk, carefulness, alignment and coverage metrics.
summary: The paper frames RAG as a risk-control problem in which the model should refuse questions it has low confidence in. It estimates confidence by counterfactually changing two factors, the quality of the retrieved passages and how they are used, and checking whether the answer changes. It builds an abstention-aware benchmark from TriviaQA and Natural Questions (RC-TQ, RC-NQ) and reports lower risk and higher carefulness than baselines. Limitation for MedBridge: it is tested on open-domain factoid QA, not clinical questions, and it has no step for asking for missing patient context or for emergency escalation.

title: C-RAG: Certified Generation Risks for Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
venue: Proceedings of the 41st International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2024), PMLR vol. 235
use_in_report: Supplementary, not the Review-1 row 6 match: it is ICML, not ACL/EMNLP Findings. Cite it next to Chen et al. 2024 in Ch.2 as the theory-side work giving certified (conformal) bounds on RAG generation risk, which motivates calibrated thresholds in MedBridge's Evidence Gate.
summary: C-RAG uses conformal risk analysis to put a provable upper confidence bound on the generation risk of retrieval-augmented models, and the bound still holds under shifts in the test distribution. It shows in theory that RAG has lower certified risk than an LLM alone when retrieval and the transformer are good enough, and confirms this on four common NLP datasets with four retrieval models. Limitation for MedBridge: it is general-domain and gives only statistical guarantees, with no clinical safety rules or escalation path.

title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
venue: Proceedings of the 16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security (AISec '23), co-located with ACM CCS '23, Copenhagen, Denmark
use_in_report: Cite in Ch.2 (security threats) and the threat-model section: it shows that RAG systems take in untrusted text from retrieved content that can carry injected instructions. This justifies MedBridge treating retrieved guideline chunks and user text as data, keeping them separate from instructions, and using deterministic gates.
summary: The paper introduces indirect prompt injection, where an attacker plants instructions in content that an LLM application later retrieves, instead of typing them in directly. It shows working attacks on real systems such as Bing Chat (GPT-4) and code-completion tools, and sorts the resulting harms into a taxonomy that includes data theft, self-spreading (worming) attacks and information contamination. It concludes that good mitigations did not exist at the time. Limitation: it demonstrates attacks rather than testing defenses, and it does not look at medical systems.

title: Formalizing and Benchmarking Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses
venue: 33rd USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 24), Philadelphia, PA, USENIX Association
use_in_report: Cite in Ch.2 and the security evaluation section as the standard formal definition and benchmark of prompt-injection attacks and defenses. It supports the claim that no single prevention or detection defense is enough, which motivates MedBridge's layered design.
summary: The paper gives a formal framework for prompt-injection attacks on LLM-integrated applications, and combines existing techniques into a stronger new attack. It benchmarks 5 attacks against 10 defenses on 10 LLMs and 7 tasks, and releases the benchmark platform publicly. It finds that the existing prevention and detection defenses tested are not enough. Limitation: it covers general tasks, not clinical or RAG-specific settings.

title: OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025
venue: OWASP Foundation, OWASP GenAI Security Project
use_in_report: Cite in Ch.2 and the security and threat-model section as the industry risk list. MedBridge's controls map onto it: LLM01 Prompt Injection (input isolation), LLM02 Sensitive Information Disclosure (PII redaction and encryption), LLM08 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses (retrieval store), LLM09 Misinformation (evidence gate and abstention).
summary: This is industry guidance, not peer reviewed. The 2025 edition ranks ten risks for LLM and GenAI applications and gives mitigations for each: prompt injection, sensitive information disclosure, supply chain, data and model poisoning, improper output handling, excessive agency, system prompt leakage, vector and embedding weaknesses, misinformation, and unbounded consumption. Limitation: it is community guidance with no empirical evaluation. A 2026 edition (published 3 Aug 2026) has since re-ranked and renumbered the risks, so the report must say it cites the 2025 version and its LLM IDs.

title: Reciprocal rank fusion outperforms condorcet and individual rank learning methods
venue: Proceedings of the 32nd International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '09)
use_in_report: System Design / Retrieval pipeline: justification for fusing the dense (BGE) and BM25 ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, the 1/(k+rank) formula and the k=60 constant; also Literature Review on rank fusion.
summary: A two-page SIGIR short paper that proposes Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which merges ranked lists by summing 1/(k + rank) for each document, and shows it beats Condorcet fusion and several learned rank-combination methods on TREC data. It needs no score calibration or training, which suits fusing dense and BM25 scores on different scales. It was tested on general web/ad-hoc TREC collections, not clinical text, and treats every ranker as equally reliable.

title: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework: BM25 and Beyond
venue: Foundations and Trends in Information Retrieval
use_in_report: Literature Review and System Design / Retrieval pipeline: the theory behind the sparse BM25 leg of the hybrid retriever (term-frequency saturation k1, length normalisation b).
summary: A survey monograph by the original BM25 authors. It explains the probabilistic relevance framework and how the binary independence model, relevance feedback, BM25 and BM25F follow from it. It is the standard reference for BM25 parameters, but it covers lexical matching only, so synonyms and paraphrases (for example 'high blood pressure' vs 'hypertension') need the dense retriever.

title: C-Pack: Packed Resources For General Chinese Embeddings
venue: Proceedings of the 47th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '24)
use_in_report: System Design / Implementation: source paper for the BGE (BAAI General Embedding) model family used as the dense embedding encoder; Literature Review on general-purpose text embeddings.
summary: Releases C-Pack, a set of resources for general text embeddings: a Chinese embedding benchmark (C-MTEB), a large training corpus, and the BGE embedding models, which were also released in English versions. The models are trained with large-scale contrastive pre-training followed by instruction-style fine-tuning. The models are general-domain, so how well they retrieve cardiology or hypertension text is not shown in the paper and has to be measured in MedBridge's own evaluation.

title: Passage Re-ranking with BERT
use_in_report: System Design / Retrieval pipeline: the reason for a second-stage cross-encoder reranker that scores each (query, passage) pair together after first-stage hybrid retrieval.
summary: Fine-tunes BERT as a cross-encoder that takes a query and a candidate passage together and outputs a relevance score, then uses it to rerank passages that BM25 retrieved. It took first place on the MS MARCO passage leaderboard at the time and gave large gains on TREC-CAR. It is an unreviewed preprint, and cross-encoder reranking is costly, since each candidate needs its own forward pass. That cost limits how many candidates a local CPU/GPU deployment can rerank.

title: MiniLM: Deep Self-Attention Distillation for Task-Agnostic Compression of Pre-Trained Transformers
venue: Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 33 (NeurIPS 2020)
use_in_report: Implementation: the backbone of the compact MiniLM-based cross-encoder reranker (e.g. an MS MARCO MiniLM cross-encoder), and why a distilled model fits a local, low-latency deployment.
summary: Compresses large Transformers by training a small student to copy the last-layer self-attention distributions and value relations of a large teacher. The students keep almost all of the teacher's accuracy on SQuAD 2.0 and GLUE with about half the parameters and compute. The paper covers general-purpose distillation only. Rerankers built on MiniLM are later fine-tuned by others on MS MARCO, so their clinical-domain ranking quality is not covered here.

title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing (EMNLP-IJCNLP)
use_in_report: Literature Review / System Design: background on bi-encoder sentence embeddings with cosine similarity, which dense retrieval is built on, and on the sentence-transformers framework used to load the embedding and cross-encoder models.
summary: Fine-tunes BERT in siamese and triplet setups so that each sentence becomes one fixed vector that can be compared with cosine similarity. This cuts semantic-search cost from pairwise cross-encoding to a single encoding per sentence plus a nearest-neighbour lookup. Bi-encoders are less precise than cross-encoders, which is why MedBridge adds a reranking stage after them.

title: DeBERTaV3: Improving DeBERTa using ELECTRA-Style Pre-Training with Gradient-Disentangled Embedding Sharing
use_in_report: Evaluation methodology: the backbone of the NLI judge (a DeBERTa-v3 model fine-tuned on NLI) used to check whether generated answer sentences are entailed by the retrieved evidence.
summary: Improves DeBERTa by pre-training it ELECTRA-style with replaced-token detection, and by adding gradient-disentangled embedding sharing so the generator and discriminator stop pulling the shared embeddings in opposite directions. DeBERTaV3-large reaches a 91.37 average on GLUE, and its NLI fine-tunes are strong entailment classifiers. The paper covers only the encoder itself. Its NLI accuracy on medical text and on long LLM answers is not measured there.

title: A Broad-Coverage Challenge Corpus for Sentence Understanding through Inference
venue: Proceedings of the 2018 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Human Language Technologies, Volume 1 (Long Papers)
use_in_report: Evaluation methodology: the NLI training corpus (MultiNLI) behind the entailment / neutral / contradiction labels the NLI judge assigns to answer sentences.
summary: Introduces MultiNLI, about 433k sentence pairs labelled entailment, neutral or contradiction across ten genres of written and spoken English, with matched and mismatched test sets for checking cross-genre generalisation. Classifiers trained on it are the usual base for NLI-based factuality checks. The genres include no clinical text, and premises are single sentences, so judging multi-sentence medical evidence is out of distribution.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
venue: Proceedings of the 2020 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)
use_in_report: Literature Review / System Design: the founding paper for learned dense retrieval with a dual encoder, as opposed to sparse BM25. It motivates the dense leg of the hybrid retriever.
summary: Trains separate BERT encoders for questions and passages with in-batch negatives, so retrieval becomes a maximum inner-product search over pre-computed passage vectors. It beats a strong Lucene BM25 baseline by 9-19 points in top-20 passage accuracy and improves end-to-end open-domain QA. It needs supervised question-passage pairs and was tested on Wikipedia QA, so it does not show robustness on rare medical terms, where lexical matching still helps.

title: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model for First Stage Ranking
venue: Proceedings of the 44th International ACM SIGIR Conference on Research and Development in Information Retrieval (SIGIR '21)
use_in_report: Literature Review / Related work on retrieval: a learned-sparse alternative to plain BM25 and dense vectors, cited when explaining why MedBridge chose BM25 + dense with RRF over a learned sparse model.
summary: Uses BERT's masked-language-model head to produce sparse term-weight vectors that include expansion terms, regularised to stay sparse, so they can be served from an inverted index like BM25. It gets effectiveness close to dense retrievers while keeping exact-term matching and index efficiency. It is a SIGIR short paper on MS MARCO, and it adds a neural model on the sparse path, which costs more than BM25 locally.

title: Another Look at DPR: Reproduction of Training and Replication of Retrieval
venue: Advances in Information Retrieval: 44th European Conference on IR Research (ECIR 2022), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer
use_in_report: System Design / Retrieval pipeline: evidence that combining dense and BM25 (sparse) retrieval in a hybrid beats either one alone, which supports MedBridge's hybrid design (the 'Lin et al. hybrid retrieval' item).
summary: An independent reproduction and replication of DPR in the Pyserini/PyGaggle toolkits. It finds that the original paper under-reported its BM25 baseline, and so also under-reported the gain from dense-sparse hybrid retrieval. Hybrids are therefore stronger than DPR's paper suggests. The experiments use open-domain Wikipedia QA, and the hybrid uses a weighted score sum rather than RRF.

title: SummaC: Re-Visiting NLI-based Models for Inconsistency Detection in Summarization
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics
use_in_report: Evaluation methodology: the design basis for the NLI judge, which splits answer and evidence into sentences, scores sentence pairs with an NLI model and aggregates them (max over evidence, then over answer sentences) to flag unsupported claims.
summary: Argues that earlier NLI-based factual-consistency checks failed because NLI models are trained on sentence pairs but were applied to whole documents. It fixes this by splitting document and summary into sentences and aggregating the pairwise NLI scores: zero-shot max-pooling (SummaCZS) or a small learned convolution over score histograms (SummaCConv). It also releases the six-dataset SummaC benchmark, where SummaCConv reached 74.4% balanced accuracy. The method was built for news summarisation, not grounded medical QA, so thresholds need recalibrating for MedBridge.

title: Qwen3 Technical Report
use_in_report: Implementation / Model selection: documents the Qwen3 open-weight model family run locally through Ollama as a generator and/or judge model.
summary: The technical report for the Qwen3 family of open-weight dense and mixture-of-experts language models. Its main feature is a single model that can switch between a step-by-step 'thinking' mode and a fast 'non-thinking' mode, with a budget on reasoning tokens. It is a vendor-written report without peer review, and its benchmarks are general-purpose, so MedBridge's own evaluation has to establish hallucination and safety behaviour in cardiology.

title: Gemma 3 Technical Report
use_in_report: Implementation / Model selection: documents the Gemma 3 open-weight models run locally through Ollama (as an alternative generator or a separate LLM-as-judge model).
summary: Describes Gemma 3, Google DeepMind's family of lightweight open-weight multimodal models, roughly 1B to 27B parameters. It adds longer context through interleaved local and global attention, and better multilingual and instruction-following behaviour. It is a vendor report on general benchmarks and does not validate clinical safety. If a Gemma model is the judge while another family generates, the report also motivates using two different model families.

title: Ollama: Run AI models locally and in the cloud
identifier: GitHub ollama/ollama (latest release v0.40.2, 2026-10-08, at time of check)
use_in_report: Implementation / System architecture: the local LLM runtime that serves Qwen3/Gemma 3 on-device, so no patient data leaves the machine (supports the privacy-first, local-LLM design claim).
summary: Ollama is an open-source MIT-licensed tool for downloading and running open-weight language models locally, behind a simple HTTP API. MedBridge uses it to keep inference on-premise for privacy. Because the project now also offers cloud-hosted models, the report should say that only local models were used, and give the exact version and model tags, since outputs can change between releases and quantisations. It is software infrastructure, not a peer-reviewed method.

title: Qdrant: Vector Search Engine
identifier: GitHub qdrant/qdrant (latest release v1.19.2, 2026-10-05, at time of check)
use_in_report: Implementation / System architecture: the vector database that stores the dense embeddings (and optionally sparse vectors and payload filters) for the hybrid retrieval stage.
summary: Qdrant is an open-source vector similarity search engine and database written in Rust under Apache 2.0. It supports payload filtering and native dense+sparse hybrid queries. MedBridge uses it as the dense index of the retrieval pipeline. It is a software reference, so the report should give the version used and whether BM25/RRF are done inside Qdrant or in the application code.

title: 2025 AHA/ACC/AANP/AAPA/ABC/ACCP/ACPM/AGS/AMA/ASPC/NMA/PCNA/SGIM Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines
use_in_report: Ch. 1/2 (clinical background) and knowledge-base design: primary US source for BP categories, measurement, treatment thresholds/targets and severe hypertension/hypertensive emergency handling; anchors the guideline corpus indexed by the RAG retriever and the thresholds used by the deterministic emergency fast-path.
summary: The current US multisociety hypertension guideline, replacing the 2017 ACC/AHA document; it covers BP measurement (office, home and ambulatory), classification, risk-based initiation of therapy, targets, special populations and severe hypertension. As a guideline it is written for clinicians, not patients, and several corrections have been issued since publication, so MedBridge's corpus must track the corrected version and cannot use it directly as patient-facing text.

title: 2024 ESC Guidelines for the management of elevated blood pressure and hypertension
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (clinical background): European counterpart to the AHA/ACC guideline; introduces the 'elevated BP' category (120-139/70-89 mmHg) and the 120-129 mmHg systolic target for treated adults; used to show that guideline definitions differ across bodies, motivating source attribution in answers.
summary: The European Society of Cardiology guideline that reframes BP as a continuum, adds an 'elevated BP' category alongside hypertension, and recommends a treated systolic target of 120-129 mmHg where tolerated. Its definitions and targets differ from US and ESH documents, so a RAG assistant that mixes sources without labelling them could give inconsistent numeric advice.

authors: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence
title: Hypertension in adults: diagnosis and management (NICE guideline NG136)
venue: National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE), London
identifier: NG136; ISBN 978-1-4731-9329-1 (published 28 August 2019; last updated 26 February 2026; earlier updates March 2022 and November 2023)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and emergency fast-path design: UK guideline whose section 1.5 (recommendation 1.5.2) defines same-day specialist referral for clinic BP of 180/120 mmHg or higher with retinal haemorrhage/papilloedema or life-threatening symptoms (new onset confusion, chest pain, signs of heart failure, acute kidney injury); supports the red-flag rules used by the deterministic escalation path.
summary: NICE's living guideline on diagnosing hypertension (with ABPM/HBPM confirmation), stepwise drug treatment, BP targets and criteria for same-day specialist review; it has been amended several times since 2019, most recently in February 2026. It is UK-specific and clinician-facing, so referral pathways and drug-step choices may not transfer directly to Indian primary care.

title: Guideline for the pharmacological treatment of hypertension in adults
use_in_report: Ch. 2 (clinical background): global, resource-sensitive recommendations on when to start drug therapy, targets, follow-up intervals, single-pill combinations and task sharing to non-physician workers; relevant to the low- and middle-income-country setting of the project.
summary: WHO's evidence-based guideline (released 24 August 2021) on drug-treatment thresholds, BP targets, choice of first-line classes, combination therapy, follow-up frequency and which health workers may start treatment. It deliberately excludes pregnancy and is pitched at health-system level, so it gives less detail on individual comorbidity scenarios than the AHA/ACC or ESC documents.

title: Global report on hypertension: the race against a silent killer
use_in_report: Ch. 1 (introduction/motivation): global burden statement that hypertension affects about 1 in 3 adults, that the number affected doubled to about 1.3 billion between 1990 and 2019, and that roughly 4 in 5 people with hypertension are not adequately treated.
summary: WHO's first global report on hypertension (19 September 2023) compiling country-level burden, treatment and control data, the health and economic consequences of uncontrolled BP, and implementation lessons from the HEARTS programme. It is a descriptive policy report based on modelled estimates rather than a clinical guideline, so it motivates the problem but should not be used as a source of treatment advice.

title: Worldwide trends in hypertension prevalence and progress in treatment and control from 1990 to 2019: a pooled analysis of 1201 population-representative studies with 104 million participants
use_in_report: Ch. 1 (motivation): epidemiological evidence that the number of adults aged 30-79 with hypertension roughly doubled from 1990 to 2019 (to about 626 million women and 652 million men) and that detection, treatment and control remain low in many countries.
summary: A Bayesian pooled analysis of 1201 population-based studies estimating hypertension prevalence, diagnosis, treatment and control for 200 countries over three decades. It shows large gaps in awareness and control, especially in low- and middle-income countries, but its estimates are modelled at population level and say nothing about how individual patients obtain or understand information.

title: 2020 International Society of Hypertension Global Hypertension Practice Guidelines
use_in_report: Ch. 2: global practice guideline offering 'essential' versus 'optimal' standards of care, useful to justify recommendations suited to resource-limited (Indian) settings.
summary: The ISH guideline gives concise worldwide recommendations, separating minimum 'essential' care for low-resource settings from 'optimal' care where resources allow. It is shorter and less granular than regional guidelines and predates the 2024-2025 updates, so its targets should be read alongside newer documents.

title: 2023 ESH Guidelines for the management of arterial hypertension The Task Force for the management of arterial hypertension of the European Society of Hypertension: Endorsed by the International Society of Hypertension (ISH) and the European Renal Association (ERA)
use_in_report: Ch. 2: second European guideline (ESH) used to illustrate inter-guideline divergence from the 2024 ESC document on BP classification and targets, which motivates per-source citation and the GENERALIZE/ABSTAIN outcomes of the Evidence Gate.
summary: The European Society of Hypertension guideline, endorsed by ISH and ERA, retains the classic BP grading and gives detailed advice on measurement, drug strategy and special populations. It differs from the 2024 ESC guideline issued a year later, which shows that even 'European guidance' is not a single source of truth for an assistant.

title: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA Guideline for the Management of Heart Failure: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines
identifier: PMID 35363499 (also published in J Am Coll Cardiol 2022;79(17):e263-e421, doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2021.12.012, PMID 35379503)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and knowledge base: comorbidity guideline for heart failure (staging, guideline-directed therapy, warning symptoms) included in the cardiology corpus and used for heart-failure red flags in the emergency fast-path.
summary: The US guideline for heart failure across stages A-D, covering diagnosis, guideline-directed medical therapy for reduced and preserved ejection fraction, devices and comorbidities. It is long and clinician-oriented, so chunking and retrieval must preserve recommendation strength and context to avoid misleading excerpts.

title: 2023 ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines
identifier: PMID 38033089; PMCID PMC11095842 (also published in J Am Coll Cardiol 2024;83(1):109-279, doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2023.08.017, PMID 38043043)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and knowledge base: atrial fibrillation guideline (hypertension as a key risk factor, stroke prevention, anticoagulation) included in the cardiology corpus; supports questions that require escalation rather than self-management advice.
summary: The joint US guideline on atrial fibrillation, which frames AF as a progressive disease with stages and emphasises risk-factor control (including BP), stroke-risk assessment, anticoagulation and rhythm/rate strategies. Many of its recommendations depend on clinician assessment and medication decisions, which a patient-facing assistant should explain but not make.

title: 2023 AHA/ACC/ACCP/ASPC/NLA/PCNA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Chronic Coronary Disease: A Report of the American Heart Association/American College of Cardiology Joint Committee on Clinical Practice Guidelines
identifier: PMID 37471501 (also published in J Am Coll Cardiol 2023;82(9):833-955, doi:10.1016/j.jacc.2023.04.003, PMID 37480922)
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and knowledge base: chronic coronary disease guideline covering BP management, lifestyle and secondary prevention for patients with coronary disease; part of the cardiology corpus and source for chest-pain escalation context.
summary: The US guideline for long-term management of chronic coronary disease, including risk-factor control (BP, lipids, diabetes), antithrombotic therapy, symptom relief and revascularisation decisions. It assumes an established diagnosis and clinician oversight, so the assistant must still escalate new or changing chest pain rather than rely on its content.

authors: Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) Blood Pressure Work Group
title: KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Blood Pressure in Chronic Kidney Disease
use_in_report: Ch. 2: example of population-specific targets (systolic BP below 120 mmHg with standardised office measurement in CKD where tolerated) that differ from general-population targets, motivating the Context Gate's SOFT-ASK for comorbidities before answering target questions.
summary: The KDIGO guideline on BP in non-dialysis CKD, notable for recommending a systolic target below 120 mmHg using standardised office measurement and for detailed advice on RAS blockade. Its target is contested and depends on careful measurement technique, so an assistant should not quote it without knowing that the user has CKD.

title: 2019 ACC/AHA Guideline on the Primary Prevention of Cardiovascular Disease: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Clinical Practice Guidelines
use_in_report: Ch. 2 and knowledge base: primary-prevention guidance on lifestyle, risk assessment and BP control; source for the lifestyle/diet/exercise questions that make up much of the patient query set.
summary: The ACC/AHA primary-prevention guideline covering team-based care, 10-year risk estimation, diet, physical activity, weight, diabetes, lipids, BP and tobacco. Its BP section relies on the 2017 hypertension guideline, which the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline has since replaced, so retrieved passages on BP thresholds may be out of date.

authors: American Diabetes Association Professional Practice Committee for Diabetes
title: 10. Cardiovascular Disease and Risk Management: Standards of Care in Diabetes—2026
identifier: PMID 41358899; PMCID PMC12690187 (published online 8 Dec 2025; 2025 edition: Diabetes Care 2025;48(Suppl 1):S207-S238, doi 10.2337/dc25-S010, PMID 39651970)
use_in_report: Ch. 2: diabetes-specific BP and cardiovascular risk guidance (targets, preferred drug classes, statins), another comorbidity that changes the correct answer and justifies context collection before answering.
summary: The ADA's annually updated section on cardiovascular risk in diabetes, covering hypertension screening and targets, lipid therapy, antiplatelet use and heart-failure/CKD considerations. It is revised every year, so the knowledge base must record the edition year to avoid mixing stale and current recommendations.

title: Metabolic non-communicable disease health report of India: the ICMR-INDIAB national cross-sectional study (ICMR-INDIAB-17)
use_in_report: Ch. 1 (Indian context): national estimate that about 35.5% of Indian adults aged 20+ have hypertension (JNC-8 criteria), plus high diabetes, obesity and dyslipidaemia prevalence, motivating a cardiometabolic assistant for Indian users.
summary: A large stratified multistage survey of 113,043 adults aged 20+ from 31 states, union territories and the National Capital Territory (2008-2020), reporting weighted prevalence of diabetes 11.4%, hypertension 35.5% and other metabolic risk factors, with urban-rural and interstate variation. Fieldwork stretched over 12 years and used JNC-8 thresholds, so figures are not directly comparable with surveys using newer definitions.

title: National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5), 2019-21: India
venue: International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai
identifier: DHS Program Final Report FR375, Volume I (cover dated March 2022; the report's suggested citation gives the year as 2021)
use_in_report: Ch. 1 (Indian context): BP measured in the national household survey shows hypertension in about 21% of women and 24% of men aged 15 and over; only 67% of women and 54% of men said their BP had ever been measured before the survey.
summary: India's national demographic and health survey report. Its adult-health chapter reports BP measured during the survey, earlier diagnosis and medication use, and finds hypertension (140/90 mmHg or above, or on BP medicine) in 21% of women and 24% of men aged 15+, with wide state variation. It includes people from age 15 and uses survey-day readings, so prevalence is not directly comparable with ICMR-INDIAB.

title: The India Hypertension Control Initiative–early outcomes in 26 districts across five states of India, 2018–2020
use_in_report: Ch. 1/2 (Indian context): describes India's national protocol-based hypertension programme (simple three-drug protocols, team-based and patient-centred care, follow-up) and its control rates, framing where a patient-education assistant could support existing public-health efforts.
summary: Reports early results of IHCI in public clinics across 26 districts of five states, where 570,365 patients were enrolled under standard three-drug protocols and clinic-level BP control averaged 43% (range 22-79%) by early 2020. It is an observational programme evaluation with documentation-dependent outcomes, and it does not test digital or AI tools.

title: 2017 ACC/AHA/AAPA/ABC/ACPM/AGS/APhA/ASH/ASPC/NMA/PCNA Guideline for the Prevention, Detection, Evaluation, and Management of High Blood Pressure in Adults: A Report of the American College of Cardiology/American Heart Association Task Force on Clinical Practice Guidelines
identifier: PMID 29133356 (also published in J Am Coll Cardiol 2018;71(19):e127-e248, doi 10.1016/j.jacc.2017.11.006, PMID 29146535). Erratum: Hypertension 2018;71(6):e140-e144
use_in_report: Ch. 2 / emergency fast-path: classic source for the distinction between hypertensive emergency (severe BP elevation, typically above 180/120 mmHg, with new or worsening target-organ damage) and hypertensive urgency; cited when justifying the fast-path thresholds and as the predecessor replaced by the 2025 guideline.
summary: The 2017 US guideline that lowered the hypertension threshold to 130/80 mmHg and set out structured definitions and management of hypertensive crises. It has been superseded by the 2025 AHA/ACC guideline, so it should be cited for historical definitions rather than as current practice.

title: Acute Severe Hypertension
use_in_report: Ch. 2 / emergency fast-path: clinical review of acute severe hypertension that separates emergencies with acute target-organ injury from severe asymptomatic hypertension; supports routing symptomatic high-BP reports to ESCALATE regardless of retrieval outcome.
summary: A clinical-practice review that defines acute severe hypertension and separates hypertensive emergencies, where there is acute organ damage, from severe BP elevation without that damage. It also covers how to evaluate patients and how to lower BP cautiously. Because it is a narrative review written for clinicians, the assistant can use it only to decide when to urge urgent care, not to guide treatment.

title: A Coefficient of Agreement for Nominal Scales
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter / IEEE Sec. on judge reliability: defines Cohen's kappa, which MedBridge uses to measure chance-corrected agreement between the LLM-as-judge and the NLI judge (and between either judge and human labels) on hallucination / supported-claim labels.
summary: Introduces kappa, an agreement index for two raters assigning items to nominal categories that subtracts the agreement expected by chance from the observed agreement. It applies to exactly two raters and categorical labels, and its value depends on how often each category occurs, so heavily imbalanced labels (e.g., very few hallucinations) can give low kappa even when raw agreement is high.

title: Note on the Sampling Error of the Difference Between Correlated Proportions or Percentages
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter / IEEE results: justifies McNemar's test for paired binary outcomes, e.g., comparing hallucination (yes/no) or correct-abstention rates of two MedBridge configurations (with vs. without the Dual Answerability Gate) on the same question set.
summary: Derives the standard error for the difference between two proportions measured on the same subjects, which leads to the test now known as McNemar's test that uses only the discordant pairs. It compares exactly two paired conditions; comparing more than two variants needs Cochran's Q, and with few discordant pairs an exact binomial version is preferable.

title: The Comparison of Percentages in Matched Samples
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter / ablation study: justifies Cochran's Q for testing whether binary outcomes (hallucinated or not, correct gate decision or not) differ across three or more MedBridge variants evaluated on the same queries.
summary: Presents the Q statistic for testing whether several matched samples share the same proportion of successes on a binary response, extending McNemar's two-sample case to k related samples. A significant Q only shows that some difference exists; pairwise post-hoc tests with a multiplicity correction (e.g., Holm) are still needed to locate it.

title: A Simple Sequentially Rejective Multiple Test Procedure
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter: multiple-comparison correction for the pairwise McNemar post-hoc tests run after a significant Cochran's Q across MedBridge ablation variants.
summary: Proposes a step-down procedure that orders p-values and tests them against progressively less strict Bonferroni-type thresholds, controlling the family-wise error rate while rejecting more hypotheses than plain Bonferroni. It controls family-wise error rather than false discovery rate, so it is conservative when many comparisons are made.

title: Probable Inference, the Law of Succession, and Statistical Inference
venue: Journal of the American Statistical Association
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter / result tables: Wilson score intervals for proportions such as hallucination rate, abstention rate, gate accuracy and emergency fast-path recall, which are often near 0 or 1 on small test sets.
summary: Derives the score-based confidence interval for a binomial proportion by inverting the normal test, which stays inside [0,1] and behaves sensibly for small samples and extreme proportions, unlike the simple Wald interval. It assumes independent trials, so correlated items (e.g., many queries from one patient scenario) make the interval too narrow.

title: An Introduction to the Bootstrap
venue: Chapman & Hall, New York (Monographs on Statistics and Applied Probability, vol. 57)
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter: bootstrap (percentile / BCa) confidence intervals for retrieval and answer metrics that lack simple closed-form intervals, e.g., Recall@k, MRR, nDCG of hybrid BM25+dense+RRF vs. dense-only retrieval.
summary: Textbook introduction to bootstrap resampling for estimating standard errors, bias and confidence intervals, including percentile and bias-corrected (BCa) intervals and bootstrap hypothesis tests. Bootstrap intervals assume the evaluation queries are a representative i.i.d. sample; with small or clustered test sets they can be unstable or too optimistic.

title: The Measurement of Observer Agreement for Categorical Data
use_in_report: Evaluation chapter: source of the commonly used kappa interpretation bands (slight, fair, moderate, substantial, almost perfect) when reporting LLM-judge vs. NLI-judge agreement.
summary: Develops a framework for assessing agreement among observers on categorical data and proposes benchmark ranges for interpreting kappa values. The benchmark bands are admittedly arbitrary conventions rather than derived thresholds, so they should be reported with that caveat.

title: The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (No. 22 of 2023)
venue: The Gazette of India, Extraordinary, Part II, Section 1, No. 25; Ministry of Law and Justice (Legislative Department), New Delhi
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter / ethics section: Indian legal basis for MedBridge's handling of patient data, including reasonable security safeguards (Sec. 8(5)), erasure on consent withdrawal or end of purpose (Sec. 8(7)), and the medical-emergency legitimate-use ground (Sec. 7(f)) relevant to the emergency fast-path.
summary: India's general data protection statute governing processing of digital personal data, setting duties for Data Fiduciaries (consent, purpose limitation, security safeguards, breach notification, erasure) and rights for Data Principals. Many operational details are left to rules notified separately, and the Act does not give health data a separate sensitive-data category, so health-specific obligations must be inferred.

authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
title: The HIPAA Privacy Rule
venue: HHS.gov (Privacy Rule located at 45 CFR Part 160 and Subparts A and E of Part 164)
identifier: 45 CFR Part 160; 45 CFR Part 164 Subparts A and E; page last reviewed 27 Sept 2024
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter / related regulation: international reference point for protecting individually identifiable health information (PHI), used to frame MedBridge's PII redaction and encryption-at-rest design.
summary: HHS overview page stating that the Privacy Rule sets national U.S. standards for protecting medical records and other individually identifiable health information, applying to health plans, health care clearinghouses and providers that conduct certain transactions electronically, and that it is codified at 45 CFR Part 160 and Subparts A and E of Part 164. It is U.S. law for covered entities, so for an Indian student project it serves as a design benchmark rather than a binding requirement.

authors: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
title: Guidance Regarding Methods for De-identification of Protected Health Information in Accordance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) Privacy Rule
venue: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, Office for Civil Rights
identifier: Dated November 26, 2012; Safe Harbor at 45 CFR 164.514(b)(2)
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter: the Safe Harbor list of 18 identifier types (names, sub-state geography, dates, phone numbers, MRNs, etc.) used to justify which entity classes MedBridge's PII redactor targets before text reaches the LLM or logs.
summary: OCR guidance explaining the two HIPAA de-identification routes, Expert Determination and Safe Harbor, where Safe Harbor removes 18 listed identifier categories (items A to R) and requires no actual knowledge that the remainder could re-identify a person. Safe Harbor is a checklist rather than a risk measure, so free-text clinical notes can still leak identity through quasi-identifiers that are not on the list.

title: Guidelines for Media Sanitization
venue: National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST Special Publication 800-88 Rev. 2
identifier: NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 2 (September 2025); supersedes SP 800-88 Rev. 1
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter: authoritative source for cryptographic erase, which supports MedBridge's crypto-shredding approach (destroying a patient's encryption key to make immutable event-sourced records unreadable) as a way to honour erasure requests.
summary: Current NIST guidance on media sanitization, describing how organizations choose sanitization techniques and build a sanitization program, with cryptographic erase among the covered topics. It targets storage media and organizational programs; applying cryptographic erase at the level of individual application records is an extension that depends on the key never having been copied elsewhere.

title: Recommendation for Key Management: Part 1 – General
venue: National Institute of Standards and Technology, NIST Special Publication 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter: guidance for generating, storing, rotating and destroying the symmetric keys used for MedBridge's encryption at rest and per-patient key crypto-shredding.
summary: General NIST recommendation on cryptographic key management, covering key types, protection requirements, cryptoperiods, key states and lifecycle functions such as generation, distribution, storage and destruction. It is written for organizational key management and does not prescribe a specific design for a single-machine local application, so MedBridge's choices must be argued against its principles.

title: Event Sourcing
use_in_report: System design chapter: pattern reference for MedBridge's event-sourced patient state, where every vitals reading, symptom report and gate decision is stored as an appended event and the current state is rebuilt by replay, giving an audit trail.
summary: Describes the event sourcing pattern, in which every change to application state is recorded as an event object stored in sequence, so state can be rebuilt, queried at past points in time, or replayed. It is a practitioner article rather than peer-reviewed work, and it does not address deleting personal data from an immutable event log, which MedBridge handles separately with crypto-shredding.

title: Ethics and governance of artificial intelligence for health: WHO guidance
use_in_report: Introduction / ethics chapter: grounds MedBridge's safety-first design (abstain and escalate rather than guess, human oversight, transparency of evidence) in WHO's six principles, such as protecting human autonomy and promoting safety and transparency.
summary: WHO guidance, produced after about eighteen months of expert consultation, that sets out ethical risks of AI in health, six consensus principles, and governance recommendations for governments, developers and providers. It predates widespread clinical use of generative LLMs (WHO issued separate guidance on large multimodal models later), so it gives principles rather than LLM-specific controls.

title: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 13 June 2024 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence and amending Regulations (EC) No 300/2008, (EU) No 167/2013, (EU) No 168/2013, (EU) 2018/858, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2019/2144 and Directives 2014/90/EU, (EU) 2016/797 and (EU) 2020/1828 (Artificial Intelligence Act)
venue: Official Journal of the European Union, L series, 2024/1689, 12.7.2024
use_in_report: Related regulation / ethics chapter: under Art. 6(1) with Annex I (which lists the Medical Devices Regulation (EU) 2017/745 and IVDR 2017/746), AI that is or is a safety component of a medical device needing third-party conformity assessment is high-risk; used to explain why MedBridge is positioned as an educational decision-support prototype with human oversight, logging and abstention.
summary: The EU's horizontal AI law, which sorts AI systems by risk and imposes requirements on high-risk systems such as risk management, data governance, logging, transparency and human oversight. It binds only systems placed on the EU market and has since been amended (see notes), so it serves as a design reference for an Indian research prototype rather than a compliance claim.

title: Presidio - Data Protection and De-identification SDK
venue: GitHub (originally developed by Microsoft; now maintained by the Data Privacy Stack community), MIT License
use_in_report: Privacy & security chapter / related work: an established open-source PII detection and anonymization framework, cited as a comparison point or possible replacement for MedBridge's own rule-based redactor.
summary: Open-source framework with analyzer and anonymizer modules that finds PII in text, images and structured data using NER models, regular expressions, checksums and context words, then redacts, replaces, masks, hashes or encrypts it. It ships recognizers for Indian identifiers (Aadhaar, PAN, passport, voter ID, vehicle registration, GSTIN), but these are turned off in the default configuration and have to be enabled. Clinical free text may still need custom recognizers or tuning.
